chunks.text: 2 Method HemaHier is an ordinal-hierarchical prediction head built on top of a cytology backbone. The key idea is to decouple three related but distinct factors of bone-marrow interpretation: fine cell identity, hematopoietic lineage, and within-lineage maturity. Figure 1 summarizes the ontology, factorized representation, chain-conditioned maturity heads, and hierarchy-conditioned inference. Bone-marrow labels are represented by fine classes, lineages, valid healthy maturation chains, and off-chain identities. A cytology backbone provides late and intermediate features, which are factorized into lineage context z c z_{c} and detail/maturity representation z d z_{d} . The coupled heads predict fine identity, lineage, and branch-conditioned maturity. Maturity supervision is applied only to valid healthy chains, while hierarchy-conditioned decoding combines fine and lineage evidence at inference. Ontology and valid maturity chains. Each fine cell type f f belongs to exactly one hematopoietic lineage, given by a fixed expert-defined mapping m ⁡ ( f ) m(f) .

Within a lineage, the healthy cell types follow a known maturation order, which we encode as a set of expert-curated chains 𝒞 q = ( u q , 0 , … , u q , n q ) , q ∈ 𝒬 , \mathcal{C}_{q}=(u_{q,0},\ldots,u_{q,n_{q}}),\qquad q\in\mathcal{Q}, (1) where u q , j u_{q,j} is the j j -th fine class of chain q q , ordered from immature ( j = 0 j{=}0 ) to mature ( j = n q j{=}n_{q} ). A cell of type u q , j u_{q,j} then receives a normalized maturity target π = j / n q ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \pi=j/n_{q}\in[0,1] . Dysplastic, atypical, and other off-chain cell types keep their lineage but lie on no chain, so they stay valid fine classes yet receive no maturity target. This avoids forcing weakly ordered or abnormal cells onto a healthy developmental axis. The same ontology also defines a maturity-aware tree distance (TD) between a predicted and a true label, used only to measure error severity, never as a training loss; it is the TD metric reported in Table 1 . A same-chain confusion costs the normalized maturity gap between the two stages, a same-lineage off-chain confusion an intermediate constant, and a cross-lineage confusion the maximum, so the metric ranks biologically mild maturation slips below severe lineage-inconsistent errors. Factorized representation. A backbone g θ g_{\theta} yields a late semantic token h L h_{L} and an intermediate morphology-preserving feature h M h_{M} . Two adapters produce a lineage context z c = ϕ c ​ ( h L ) z_{c}=\phi_{c}(h_{L}) and a detail representation z d = ϕ d ​ ( [ h L ; h M ] ) z_{d}=\phi_{d}([h_{L};h_{M}]) that captures chromatin texture, granularity, and within-lineage maturity cues; the fine representation is their concatenation [ z c ; z d ] [z_{c};z_{d}] . Coupled heads and consistent posterior. Rather than predicting fine class and lineage independently, HemaHier couples them into a single lineage-consistent posterior.

At test time we decode each cell from the hierarchy-consistent posterior p f ​ ( f ∣ x ) p_{f}(f\mid x) , which by construction keeps the predicted fine class and its lineage in agreement. Optionally, this posterior can be recalibrated by the chain-conditioned maturity score, favouring fine classes whose expected maturation position matches the predicted one. Models are selected on validation macro-F1 under the hierarchy-consistent posterior. 3 Experimental results 3.1 Setup Datasets and ontology. We evaluate on two in-house bone-marrow cytology datasets, UKA2 (9,118 cells, 23 fine classes) and UKA1 (8,566 cells, 24 fine classes), and the public MLLv1 (BMC) bone-marrow reference [ 15 ] (171,374 cells, 21 fine classes). Dataset-specific labels are harmonized into a shared ontology of fine identities, lineages, healthy maturation chains, and off-chain variants. Each fine class maps to one lineage, and maturity targets are defined only for biologically valid healthy chains; atypical, dysplastic, and ambiguous identities remain valid fine classes but are excluded from maturity supervision. Protocol and baselines.

We use five-fold stratified cross-validation per dataset, sharing splits, preprocessing, augmentation, sampler, optimizer, and training budget across all methods. Unless noted, the backbone is DinoBloom-S [ 13 ] , a compact hematology foundation model; our method is backbone-agnostic, and we refer to it simply as the backbone below. A shared frozen backbone isolates the effect of the prediction head; we additionally report a LoRA-adapted [ 10 ] (rank 16) backbone. Because public bone-marrow splits differ across works, all methods are re-trained and evaluated under our common five-fold protocol, and checkpoints are selected by validation macro-F1. We compare against a flat linear probe, the standard foundation-model evaluation protocol, and HMIL ∗ , our single-cell adaptation of the hierarchical multi-instance framework of Jin et al. [ 12 ] : the original aggregates a bag of patches by attention [ 11 ] for whole-slide images, which degenerates when each image is a single cell, so we retain its coarse/fine hierarchical head and train it on the same features as every method. The ablation additionally includes a multi-scale flat variant that reads the same features without the hierarchy. Implementation and metrics. Models use 224 × 224 224\times 224 crops with the backbone’s standard preprocessing, AdamW (weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} ), batch size 64, 20 epochs, a cosine schedule with linear warmup, and learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} ; the adapted setting uses LoRA [ 10 ] rank 16. The lineage, maturity, and ranking losses use weights λ c = 0.05 \lambda_{c}{=}0.05 , λ m = 0.005 \lambda_{m}{=}0.005 , and λ r = 0.003 \lambda_{r}{=}0.003 , ramped in after warmup, and the auxiliary fine cross-entropy weight is increased under adaptation.

On top of the frozen backbone ( 21.6 21.6 M parameters), the HemaHier head adds 5.0 5.0 M trainable parameters, and under adaptation a rank-16 LoRA adds a further 0.44 0.44 M; the backbone is never fully fine-tuned, and the chain-conditioned maturity components that produce the ordinal axis account for under 0.25 0.25 M of the added parameters. Experiments ran on NVIDIA TITAN RTX GPUs. For recognition we report accuracy, balanced accuracy, fine and rare-class macro-F1, and weighted F1. For error severity we use the cross-lineage error rate (CLE) and the maturity-aware tree distance (TD) from Sec. 2 , and we assess maturation quality by the Spearman correlation and pairwise order accuracy between predicted and reference positions on healthy on-chain cells. 3.2 Results We evaluate HemaHier against a flat linear probe and the HMIL ∗ method on three bone-marrow cytology datasets under a frozen backbone, where every method shares identical features and only the prediction head differs, and a lightly LoRA-adapted backbone (Table 1 ). On the frozen backbone every method reads identical features, so differences primarily reflect the prediction head. HemaHier attains the best fine and rare-class F1 on UKA2 and MLLv1, by far the largest margin on the rare-class-imbalanced MLLv1, where it improves fine macro-F1 by 8.9 8.9 points ( → 72.2 63.3\!\to\!72.2 ) and rare-class F1 by over twenty points ( → 59.1 38.6\!\to\!59.1 ) over the strongest baseline; the MLLv1 recognition gains and the cross-lineage-error reductions on all three datasets are significant (paired t t -test over folds, p < 0.05 p<0.05 ). On UKA1 the methods are tied on macro-F1 (within the cross-fold deviation), as several classes contribute only one or two cells per fold; HemaHier still leads on the more stable accuracy, weighted F1, and both severity metrics, and adds a maturity read-out a flat classifier cannot express. LoRA adaptation . With a rank-16 adapter and a strengthened auxiliary fine cross-entropy that keeps adaptation recognition-driven, HemaHier attains the best accuracy and fine and rare-class F1 on all three datasets (e.g. + 1.6 +1.6 macro-F1 and + 4.2 +4.2 rare-class F1 over the adapted flat probe on MLLv1) together with the lowest cross-lineage and tree-distance errors, so the structural advantages persist under adaptation. The margin narrows on the pathology-heavy UKA1, where one lineage dominates and many cells are blasts, dysplastic, or off-chain, so the lineage prior has little to disambiguate; there HemaHier still leads the flat probe and HMIL ∗ on accuracy, weighted F1, macro-F1, and both severity metrics, and uniquely provides a calibrated maturation ordering ( ρ = 0.89 \rho{=}0.89 ).

Figure 2 : Errors are fewer and milder (frozen backbone, 5-fold mean). Each bar is the fine-classification error rate decomposed by clinical severity, from an adjacent-stage maturation slip (mildest) to a cross-lineage confusion (severest). On every dataset HemaHier both shortens the bar (fewer errors) and shrinks its severe (dark) portion relative to the flat probe, most visibly the cross-lineage errors on MLLv1 and the off-chain confusions on UKA1. Error severity. Clinically, how a model errs matters: a same-lineage maturation slip is far milder than a cross-lineage confusion. Decomposing errors by severity (Fig. 2 ), HemaHier makes fewer and milder mistakes, with the lowest cross-lineage error and tree distance across datasets. Maturity structure. The chain-conditioned maturity head recovers a continuous within-chain ordering rather than only discrete labels. Across three datasets, it achieves competitive recognition, with particularly strong rare-class performance on the most imbalanced dataset, while making residual errors that are biologically more plausible: lower cross-lineage error and tree distance at a fixed recognition budget. Beyond labels, it recovers a calibrated within-lineage maturity ordering that flat classifiers cannot express, and its hierarchy-consistent decoder can trade toward lineage safety at inference without retraining. Its main limitation is reliance on expert-curated maturation chains, a natural target for future extension to pathological trajectories.
